title: Theo and the Alibi
premise: Paloma Lockridge is hired to verify the death of Marisol Vega, a key witness who vanished before testifying against the Calloway shipping family, and whose diary—Paloma's only evidence—keeps being written after her supposed drowning. Following entries that reference places only Marisol could know, Paloma uncovers a witness-protection scheme gone wrong and a second investigator who faked the death to protect her. In the climax at an abandoned cannery, Paloma finds Marisol alive but must choose between closing the case with a lie or exposing the found family that hid her; they choose truth on their own terms, testifying alongside Marisol as the trial begins.
about_author: Odile Amberdale is the pen name of a former maritime insurance clerk who spent a decade reading other people's loss reports before writing her own. She lives in a fog-bound coastal town where she keeps meticulous notebooks she claims are fiction.

chapters.title: The File That Wouldn't Close
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. A routine death-verification case lands on their desk: Marisol Vega, drowned, case closed by another firm. Paloma's photographic memory flags a discrepancy in the tide charts within minutes. Emotional beat: professional pride curdling into unease as they accept the file no one else wants.

chapters.title: Diary of a Drowned Woman
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Examining Marisol's recovered diary, Paloma finds entries dated eleven days past the drowning—handwriting identical, details impossible to fake. Their boss urges them to sign off anyway. Beat: the first crack in Paloma's faith in paperwork and in themselves.

chapters.title: The Widow Who Smiled Wrong
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Interviewing Marisol's sister-in-law Rosa in the fishing village of Puerto Sombra, Paloma notices grief performed too precisely, like a rehearsed statement. A neighbor mentions a stranger's boat the night Marisol vanished. Beat: suspicion shifts from tragedy to conspiracy.

chapters.title: Calloway & Sons
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Digging into the defendants, Paloma learns the Calloway shipping empire has buried three prior witnesses under 'accidents.' Their memory recalls a face from a years-old claims photo: the other investigator on the case, one Denny Marsh. Beat: dread—the case has a history of eating investigators.

chapters.title: A Man Called Marsh
chapters.summary: Denny's POV, first time. In a rented room two hundred miles away, Denny burns a photograph and checks the locks twice. He knows someone is pulling Marisol's thread. Beat: fear and fierce protectiveness, revealing him as guardian rather than villain.

chapters.title: Entries After the End
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The later diary entries describe a lighthouse, a tin of lemon drops, a scar on a left hand—details matching nothing in the official file but everything in a postcard Paloma tracks to a shuttered cannery town. Beat: exhilaration of the hunt overtaking caution.

chapters.title: The Firm's Quiet Man
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma's supervisor, Mr. Ellery Hale, warns them off with unusual gentleness—and Paloma's memory retrieves the moment Hale once took a call from a Calloway number. Beat: betrayal; the institution Paloma trusted may be compromised.

chapters.title: Lemon Drops at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. In Grayhaven, the cannery town, a shopkeeper remembers a woman buying lemon drops every Friday—a habit from the diary's final entry. Someone watches Paloma from across the street. Beat: the hunt turns hunted; adrenaline and isolation.

chapters.title: What the Sea Kept
chapters.summary: Rosa's POV. Flashback chapter: Rosa confessing to the reader what really happened the night of the 'drowning'—the boat, the staged scene, and why she lied for a sister-in-law she barely knew. Beat: guilt and love entangled, reframing the whole mystery.

chapters.title: Two Investigators, One Lie
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma corners Denny Marsh at a dockside bar. He neither confirms nor denies, but slips them a matchbook from the cannery before vanishing. Beat: grudging mutual recognition between two people who live by observation.

chapters.title: The Trial Date
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. News breaks: the Calloway trial is moved up six weeks. Without Marisol, the prosecution collapses. Paloma realizes whoever moved the date wants the witness dead or silent forever. Beat: ticking clock installed; stakes become public and irreversible.

chapters.title: Hale's Ledger
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Breaking into the firm's archive, Paloma reconstructs Hale's payments from a shell company tied to Calloway—and finds their own name already added to a list of 'exposures.' Beat: cold terror; invisibility was never an option.

chapters.title: The Woman in the Window
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV, first time. Alive in a cannery loft, Marisol watches the stranger (Paloma) photograph her lighthouse and debates running again. She writes a new diary entry addressed to whoever is looking. Beat: weary hope; the hunted considering trust.

chapters.title: Matchbook
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Following the matchbook to the cannery, Paloma trips a wire alarm and meets Denny at gunpoint in the dark. Standoff becomes negotiation: Denny shows proof of the Calloway threats that forced the fake death. Beat: enemies becoming reluctant allies.

chapters.title: Found Family
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol confronts Denny about bringing an outsider in; the argument reveals their years of hiding together—safe houses, coded grocery lists, birthdays celebrated with stolen candles. Beat: tenderness inside danger; Paloma watching, aching with envy of belonging.

chapters.title: The Photograph
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma's memory finally places the crucial image: a claims photo proving a Calloway executive met Hale the week before the 'drowning.' But using it means exposing how Paloma obtained it—and burning their career. Beat: loyalty vs. truth made personal.

chapters.title: Hale Comes Calling
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Hale offers Paloma a partnership and the case closed clean—if they hand over the diary. Paloma plays along long enough to record his admission, then walks out knowing he'll send someone. Beat: quiet courage; the point of no return.

chapters.title: Night at the Cannery
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs interwoven. Hale's fixers raid the cannery; Denny holds the loading door while Marisol escapes through the fish chute and Paloma uses the building's mirrored walls—memory turned weapon—to mislead the searchers. Beat: climax; chaos, sacrifice, Denny wounded covering the retreat.

chapters.title: The Witness Everyone Swears Is Dead
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Paloma delivers Marisol—not to hiding, but to the prosecutor's doorstep—with the recorded ledger, the photograph, and the diary complete through its true final entry. Beat: catharsis; truth chosen over safety, together rather than alone.

chapters.title: Testimony
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. On the stand, Marisol identifies the Calloways while Paloma's photographic recall dismantles the defense's timeline from the gallery. Hale is arrested leaving the courthouse. Beat: vindication earned collectively; the dead woman speaking.

chapters.title: What Paloma Closed
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The verdict lands; Paloma resigns from the firm rather than return to its ledgers, keeping only the Vega file. Denny, recovering, offers grudging respect; Rosa invites Paloma to Sunday dinner. Beat: bittersweet release; the investigator learning to be witnessed.

chapters.title: A New Entry
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV, closing frame. Marisol begins a fresh notebook, first line addressed to Paloma: 'For the one who read to the end.' The found family gathers at the lighthouse as fog lifts. Beat: warmth and continuation; identity rebuilt not in hiding but in company.
